title: Floating Star Driveway
subject: Torts
subtopic: Standard of Due Care / Best Argument
stem:
Source row: BARMATRIX Q# 20439 is a Torts item with official key B. The supplied original answer set tests the walker’s best tort argument against a professional dog trainer: strict product liability for use of a defective product, unreasonable front-yard activity, concurring cause, and professional status. The official explanation identifies unreasonable conduct as the only listed argument that could support liability.

Christian variation — QID 20439_floating_star_driveway

Timothy was walking on the public sidewalk past Lydia’s house on Saturday morning. Lydia, a professional director of children’s Christmas pageants, was rehearsing a “floating star” scene for a neighborhood Advent program. She tested a rented battery-powered cable rig in her open driveway beside the sidewalk. A defect in the rig caused a plywood star to swing outside the driveway and strike Timothy.

If Timothy asserts a claim against Lydia, Timothy’s most effective argument in support of his claim would be that
call: If Timothy asserts a claim against Lydia, Timothy’s most effective argument in support of his claim would be that

choices.A: Lydia was a professional Christmas-pageant director.
choices.B: Lydia’s conduct was a concurring cause of Timothy’s harm.
choices.C: It was unreasonable for Lydia to test the cable rig in her open driveway beside a public sidewalk.
choices.D: Lydia is strictly liable for harm resulting from her use of a defective product.

rightExplanation: C is correct. Timothy’s strongest listed argument is that Lydia acted unreasonably by testing the cable rig in an open driveway beside a public sidewalk. Gold Key: negligence needs an unreasonable-risk theory; here, the argument supplies a fault basis instead of merely pointing to a product, a cause, or Lydia’s professional title. Silver Key: on a “most effective argument” call, do not demand a guaranteed win. Choose the only answer that gives the plaintiff a legally operative route to liability.

c3.label: CUT A — professional status
c3.text: Status alone does not answer the call. It says what Lydia is, not what she did wrong. Cut as NOT_RESPONSIVE, wrong_element.

c3.label: CUT B — concurring cause
c3.text: Cause alone is incomplete. The claim needs an operative liability basis. Cut as NOT_RESPONSIVE, wrong_element.

c3.label: CUT D — defective product strict liability
c3.text: This uses a real neighboring doctrine but points it at the wrong role. Lydia is the user in the stem, not the commercial supplier. Cut as NOT_RESPONSIVE, bait_doctrine, anchor-assisted.

c3.label: Residual C
c3.text: C gives the only argument that supplies unreasonable conduct. No CLASH remains. CALL not needed beyond the best-argument navigation check.

studentScript: Best argument for Timothy. Product defect is tempting, but Lydia is a user. Cause is only cause. Professional title is only status. Unreasonable testing beside the sidewalk gives negligence. Pick C.

A.signal: The answer gives who Lydia is, not what she did wrong.
A.lawyer: Professional status may inform the standard of care, but status alone does not establish breach.

B.signal: The answer supplies causal connection, but not a liability basis.
B.lawyer: Causation is necessary but not sufficient; liability requires negligence, intent, or strict-liability category.

C.signal: The answer gives a blame/fault theory that responds to the claim-support call.
C.lawyer: Unreasonable conduct is the breach/fault route for negligence.

D.signal: The product-defect words are real, but the stem casts Lydia as a user.
D.lawyer: Strict products liability runs against commercial sellers/distributors, not a mere user of the product.

goldKeys.statement: Strict products liability for a defective product is aimed at commercial sellers or distributors, not a person who merely uses the product.
goldKeys.trigger: The defendant is using, testing, or operating a product rather than selling or distributing it.

goldKeys.statement: Cause and status are not enough; the plaintiff’s argument must supply negligence, intent, or a strict-liability category. Unreasonable conduct supplies the negligence route.
goldKeys.trigger: A best-argument call with choices that name cause, status, or product defect.
goldKeys.unlocks: Separates the fault-basis answer from cause-only and status-only distractors.
goldKeys.authority: Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm § 3.

silverKeys.statement: On a best-argument call, pick the answer that gives the plaintiff a legal route to liability; do not require the answer to prove the whole case.
silverKeys.trigger: The call asks for the claimant’s most effective argument.
silverKeys.unlocks: The gap between possible liability and guaranteed liability.

remediation.title: Cause/status/product are not the claim
remediation.signal: A Torts answer names only cause, status, or product defect.
remediation.studentMove: Ask whether the answer supplies a liability basis.
remediation.tinyRule: For negligence, look for unreasonable conduct.
remediation.trap: Choosing a legally flavored fragment instead of the operative ground.
